title: English Vocabulary 1 · Units 39–40
description: Unit 39 covers movement with go/went/gone, destination and direction expressions, going to for future plans and go + -ing activities. Unit 40 covers auxiliary and main-verb do/did/done, questions and negatives, short answers, jobs and common do collocations. Each entry has a Portuguese translation in pt and an original English example.

units.title: Unit 39 — Go / went / gone
units.source: Vocabulary study targets from published reference material; Unit 39. Page information, if available, is retained in sourceAudit.

items.pt: ir; fui/foi; ido (formas do verbo irregular)
items.example: We went to the cinema yesterday.
items.note: Go is irregular: go (base form), went (past simple), gone (past participle). Have gone often suggests that someone is still away; have been can describe a completed visit.

items.pt: ir a um lugar; ir para um lugar
items.example: I go to the library after school.
items.note: Use go to before a named destination or place: go to London, go to the swimming pool. Do not add to before home, there, somewhere or anywhere.

items.example: She goes to work at eight every day.
items.note: Go to work means travel to your workplace or begin work. In this common phrase, work does not usually take the.

items.example: I sometimes go to work by bike.
items.note: Use by + mode of transport without an article: by bike, by train or by car.

items.example: My neighbours go to the city by car.
items.note: Use by + transport without a or the: go by car. The teaching page contrasts travelling by bike and by car.

items.example: My parents went to Bristol last month.
items.note: A named city can follow go to: go to London or go to Paris. Place names have their own pronunciations.

items.example: Would you like to go to the swimming pool this afternoon?
items.note: Go to the swimming pool names a destination. Go swimming names the activity, without to.

items.example: Where does this road go? Does it reach the village?
items.note: Go can describe where a road or route leads. After the auxiliary does, use the base form go, not goes.

items.example: Excuse me, where does this bus go?
items.note: Ask Where does this bus go? to check its destination. Do not use goes after does. This question also appears in an exercise.

items.example: We are going to the zoo on Saturday.
items.note: Go to the zoo names a destination. The pictured travel exercise uses be going to + a place, which describes movement and is different from a future plan followed by a verb.

items.example: It was cold outside, so we went in.
items.note: Go in can stand alone when the destination is understood. Go into is normally followed by a place, such as a room.

items.example: The children went into the classroom quietly.
items.note: Into expresses movement to the inside of a place: go into the room or go into the garden.

items.example: He went out of the shop and crossed the road.
items.note: Use out of to express movement from inside to outside: go out of the shop. Out off is incorrect here.

items.example: She went up the stairs to the first floor.
items.note: Up indicates movement to a higher level. Contrast go up the stairs with go down the stairs.

items.example: He went down the stairs to open the door.
items.note: Down indicates movement to a lower level. Contrast go down the stairs with go up the stairs.

items.example: The dog wanted to go out into the garden.
items.note: Go out can be used without a destination. Depending on the context, it can mean leave a building or go somewhere socially.

items.example: We went up to the top of the hill.
items.note: Use go up when moving towards a higher point. In the correction exercise, down to the top is inconsistent with this intended movement.

items.pt: ter a intenção de fazer algo; ir fazer algo (plano futuro)
items.section: C · Future plans: be going to
items.example: I am going to study tonight.
items.note: Be + going to + base verb often expresses a future plan or intention. Be going to + place can describe movement towards that place instead.

items.section: C · Future plans: be going to
items.example: I’m going to visit my cousin next weekend.
items.note: I’m is short for I am. After going to in a future-plan construction, use the base form of the verb.

items.pt: vai fazer algo (terceira pessoa do singular)
items.section: C · Future plans: be going to
items.example: My sister is going to learn French this year.
items.note: Use is with he, she, it and singular subjects. The future-plan exercise practises Victoria is going to + base verb.

items.pt: vamos/vão fazer algo; você vai fazer algo
items.section: C · Future plans: be going to
items.example: We are going to watch a film after dinner.
items.note: Use are going to with you, we and they. Follow it with a base verb to express a plan.
items.speechText: we are going to watch a film

items.section: C · Future plans: be going to
items.example: He is going to study engineering at university.
items.note: Be going to study expresses an intention to study. It is not the same as going to a university building.

items.section: C · Future plans: be going to
items.example: We are going to visit our aunt in May.
items.note: Visit takes a direct object: visit my aunt, not visit to my aunt. Be going to visit expresses a planned visit.

items.section: C · Future plans: be going to
items.example: My New Year’s resolutions include reading more books.
items.note: A New Year’s resolution is a decision to make a change in the coming year. This expression appears in the future-plans exercise.

items.section: C · Future plans: be going to
items.example: I’m going to stop eating sweets after dinner.
items.note: This is a pattern from the resolutions exercise: be going to + stop + -ing. Say stop eating, not stop to eat, when you mean give up eating something.
items.speechText: I am going to stop eating chocolate

items.example: On holiday, we often go swimming in the morning.
items.note: For many leisure activities, use go + -ing: go swimming, go shopping, go skiing. The IPA gives only go because the activity verb varies.

items.example: We usually go shopping on Friday evenings.
items.note: Go shopping means spend time buying or looking for things to buy. Do not say go to shopping or go for shopping in this use.

items.example: I go swimming before work twice a week.
items.note: Use go swimming for the activity, without to or for. Compare go to the swimming pool for the destination.

items.example: Would you like to go dancing on Saturday?
items.note: Go + -ing can name a leisure activity. Go dancing means go somewhere to dance.

items.example: We went sightseeing during our holiday.
items.note: Sightseeing means visiting interesting places, especially as a tourist. Use go sightseeing, not go sightsee, for this activity.

items.example: My friends go skiing every winter.
items.note: Use go skiing for the activity. The -ing form of ski is skiing, with two consecutive i letters.

items.example: My grandfather goes fishing by the river.
items.note: Use go fishing for the activity. The correction exercise contrasts this with the unnatural go to fish in this context.

items.pt: ir fazer compras (forma com -ing de go)
items.example: She is going shopping this afternoon.
items.note: The first -ing form is the present participle of go; shopping names the activity. The whole phrase can be used in the present continuous.

items.pt: ir para casa; voltar para casa
items.section: Common mistakes · Place adverbs and contrasts
items.example: I need to go home before ten.
items.note: Home acts as a direction word here: say go home, without to or at.

items.section: Common mistakes · Place adverbs and contrasts
items.example: We go there every summer.
items.note: There already indicates a destination: say go there, not go to there.

items.section: Common mistakes · Place adverbs and contrasts
items.example: This café is full, so let’s go somewhere else.
items.note: Somewhere is an adverb of place: go somewhere else, not go to somewhere else.

items.pt: ir a qualquer outro lugar; ir para outro lugar
items.section: Common mistakes · Place adverbs and contrasts
items.example: I do not want to go anywhere else today.
items.note: Anywhere commonly appears in questions and negative statements. Do not place to immediately before anywhere in this construction.

items.section: Common mistakes · Place adverbs and contrasts
items.example: Please go away; I need to study.
items.note: Go away means leave or move away. Do not add to before away.

learningObjectives: Use go, went and gone accurately for movement, destinations, means of transport and routes.
Distinguish go to + a destination from go by + a means of transport, and use go home, go there, go somewhere and go anywhere without to.
Describe movement with in, into, out of, up and down, and correct out off or down to the top where inappropriate.
Express future plans with am/is/are going to + a base verb, distinguishing this from be going to + a place.
Use go + -ing for leisure activities such as shopping, swimming, dancing, sightseeing, skiing and fishing.
Apply these patterns to travel routes, plans, holiday activities and common errors in exercises 39.1–39.5.

units.title: Unit 40 — Do / did / done
units.source: Vocabulary study targets from published reference material; Unit 40. Page information, if available, is retained in sourceAudit.

items.pt: fazer; fiz/fez; feito (formas do verbo irregular)
items.example: I did the washing yesterday, but I have not done the ironing yet.
items.note: Do is irregular: do (base form), did (past simple), done (past participle). It can function both as a main verb and as an auxiliary.

items.example: Do you like this programme?
items.note: As an auxiliary in present-simple questions and negatives, do does not mean perform an action. Use the base form of the main verb after it.

items.pt: auxiliar da terceira pessoa do singular (presente)
items.example: Does your brother play tennis?
items.note: Use does with he, she, it and singular subjects. The main verb stays in the base form: Does she work?, not Does she works?

items.pt: auxiliar de perguntas e negativas no passado
items.example: Did they enjoy the concert?
items.note: Did marks the past simple in questions and negatives. Use the base form after did: Did you go?, not Did you went?

items.example: Do you watch TV in the evening?
items.note: Use Do + subject + base verb? to make present-simple questions with I, you, we and they.

items.example: Did they enjoy their holiday?
items.note: Did already marks the past. The main verb in a question must remain in the base form.

items.example: “Do you read the news online?” “Yes, I do.”
items.note: A short answer repeats the auxiliary, rather than the full main verb. Compare Yes, I do and No, I don’t.

items.example: “Did they go to the museum?” “Yes, they did.”
items.note: A positive short answer about a past action uses did. Compare No, they didn’t.

items.example: I enjoy music, and so does my sister.
items.note: Use So does + a singular third-person subject to agree with a positive present-simple statement: I like music, and so does my sister.

items.example: “I liked the exhibition.” “So did I.”
items.note: Use So did I to agree with a positive past-simple statement. For the present simple, use So do I.

items.example: I don’t watch reality TV.
items.note: Use do not or don’t + base verb for negative present-simple statements with I, you, we and they.

items.pt: não (negação na terceira pessoa do singular)
items.example: She doesn’t live near the station.
items.note: Use doesn’t + base verb with he, she and it. Say she doesn’t live, not she don’t live or she doesn’t lives.

items.example: They didn’t go to Wales last year.
items.note: Use didn’t + base verb for all subjects in past-simple negatives: didn’t go, not didn’t went.

items.pt: não joga; não toca (terceira pessoa singular)
items.example: He doesn’t play football very well.
items.note: After doesn’t, keep the main verb in the base form play, not plays.

items.example: I didn’t see your message this morning.
items.note: After didn’t, use see, not saw. The auxiliary carries the past-tense meaning.

items.section: B · Do as a general verb
items.example: What can I do to help you?
items.note: As a main verb, do can mean carry out or perform an action. This differs from auxiliary do in questions and negatives.

items.section: B · Do as a general verb
items.example: On Sundays I like to do nothing and rest.
items.note: Nothing already makes the meaning negative: do nothing is correct. Do not nothing is not standard English.

items.section: B · Do as a general verb
items.example: Don’t do that! You might break the glass.
items.note: The first do is an auxiliary that forms a negative command; the second do is the main verb meaning perform an action.

items.section: B · Do as a general verb
items.example: What are you doing? Are you painting the wall?
items.note: Use the present continuous to ask about an activity in progress. What do you do? often asks about a person’s occupation.

items.section: B · Do as a general verb
items.example: They are doing something interesting in the garden.
items.note: Doing is the -ing form of do. With a form of be, it can describe an action in progress.

items.section: B · Do as a general verb
items.example: I cannot clean the kitchen now; I will do it later.
items.note: Do it can refer back to an activity already mentioned. Later means at a future time.

items.pt: Qual é sua profissão?; O que você faz da vida?
items.example: “What do you do?” “I’m an engineer.”
items.note: In a conversation about jobs, What do you do? asks about someone’s occupation, not what they are doing right now.

items.example: “What does she do?” “She’s a doctor.”
items.note: Use does as the auxiliary and do as the main verb: What does she do?, not What does she does?

items.example: “What’s your job?” “I’m a teacher.”
items.note: This direct question asks about someone’s occupation. The book gives it as an explanation of What do you do?

items.example: What did you do after class?
items.note: The first word did is an auxiliary marking the past; do is the base form of the main verb. This pattern is practised in the exercise about past activities.

items.example: We do the housework together on Saturdays.
items.note: Housework is normally uncountable. Do the housework means complete household tasks such as cleaning and tidying.

items.example: My grandfather does the gardening every weekend.
items.note: Do the gardening means work in a garden. Do gardening is also possible; make the gardening is not natural.

items.example: I did the washing before breakfast.
items.note: In British English, do the washing usually means wash clothes. Do the washing-up means wash dishes.

items.example: Could you do the washing-up after dinner?
items.note: In British English, do the washing-up means wash dishes and related kitchen items. Compare do the washing for clothes.

items.pt: fazer a lição de casa; fazer a tarefa
items.example: Please do your homework before the film starts.
items.note: Use do with homework, not make. Homework is normally uncountable: some homework, not a homework.

items.example: We do some English exercises in every lesson.
items.note: Use do some exercises for practice tasks. In some contexts, exercise can also be uncountable when it means physical activity.

items.example: Our company does business with firms in Europe.
items.note: Use do business with + a person, company or organisation to describe commercial dealings. Business is generally uncountable in this sense.

items.word: do a lot of business with
items.pt: ter muitas relações comerciais com; fazer muitos negócios com
items.example: The manufacturer does a lot of business with local shops.
items.note: A lot of emphasises how much business is done. This is a longer form of do business with.

items.pt: fazer o seu melhor; esforçar-se ao máximo
items.example: You have prepared well, so do your best in the interview.
items.note: Do your best means make the greatest effort you can. Do not say make your best. The past form is did my best.

items.pt: lavou a roupa; fez a lavagem de roupas
items.example: Did you do the washing yesterday?
items.note: Did is the past form of main-verb do in statements. In questions with auxiliary did, say Did you do the washing?, not Did you did the washing?

items.example: I do a lot of housework during the week.
items.note: A lot of can modify uncountable housework. This phrase is also practised in the exercise about household activities.

learningObjectives: Recognise do, did and done as irregular verb forms and distinguish auxiliary do from main-verb do.
Form present- and past-simple questions, negatives and short answers with do, does and did, followed by a base verb.
Use So does ... and So did I to agree with positive statements in the appropriate tense.
Distinguish What are you doing? about a current activity from What do you do? about occupation.
Use common do collocations for housework, gardening, washing, washing-up, homework, exercises, business and doing your best.
Apply do/does/did agreement and base-verb forms correctly in the job, action and error-correction exercises.
